title: David's Kingdom Takes Root
overview: While the ark still waits to be brought to Jerusalem, David's rule is confirmed by a foreign king's help, a growing family, and two victories over the Philistines.

parts.label: A palace from Tyre (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Tyre was a wealthy port city to the north, famous for cedar wood and skilled builders, so Hiram's gift showed that neighbouring rulers now treated David as a real king. David took this as a sign that God had made his kingship secure, and that it was meant to serve his people rather than himself.

parts.label: David's family grows (vv. 3-7)
parts.note: Kings of that time often took many wives to show power and build alliances, though Israel's own law warned kings against it, and many readers see this as a weakness in David. Solomon, the son who would later rule after him, appears in the list.

parts.label: First Philistine attack (vv. 8-12)
parts.note: The Philistines, Israel's longtime enemy on the coast, tried to crush David before his rule was settled, but he asked God first and won near Jerusalem, saying God had burst through his enemies like a flood. The place came to be called Baal Perazim, meaning roughly "lord of breaking through," and David had the idols the Philistines left behind burned, as Israel's law required.

parts.label: Second attack and victory (vv. 13-16)
parts.note: This time God told David to circle around the enemy and wait for a sound like marching in the treetops, the signal that God had gone out ahead of him. The exact type of tree is uncertain, and the victory, stretching from Gibeon to Gezer, drove the Philistines back from the hill country toward their own lowlands.

parts.label: David's fame spreads (v. 17)
parts.note: The chapter closes by crediting the LORD with making David respected and feared among the nations. Christians later read David's widening reputation as a picture of the honour they believe belongs to Jesus, often called the Son of David.

think: When things start going well for someone, what helps them remember who their success is supposed to serve?
